\begin{frame}{What Statistics of Financial Markets Studies}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Statistics of financial markets}: statistical methods for prices, returns and risks of traded assets
    \begin{itemize}
        \item describe: how large and how variable are returns?
        \item model: which distribution, which dependence over time?
        \item measure risk: how large can a loss be on a bad day?
    \end{itemize}
    \item Why financial data need their own methods
    \begin{itemize}
        \item extreme days are far more frequent than the Normal distribution predicts (\emph{heavy tails})
        \item calm and turbulent periods alternate (\emph{volatility clustering})
        \item markets fall together in crises: diversification weakens when it is most needed
    \end{itemize}
    \item These regularities are the \emph{stylised facts} of returns (\refCont), studied in \sfmchlink{https://danpele.github.io/SFM/EN/Courses/chapter2_classical_distributions_stylised_facts.pdf}{Chapter 2}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{AI Policy}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{AI tools are allowed and must be declared}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item AI: artificial intelligence; here, assistants based on an LLM (large language model) that write text and code
        \item every use goes into \texttt{AI\_USE.md}: the tool, the request, what was kept, what was corrected
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{You are responsible for every number and every reference}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item typical AI errors: invented references, wrong formulas, code that runs but computes the wrong thing
        \item every reference: open its DOI (Digital Object Identifier) and check the title
        \item every number: recompute it with your own code from the course data
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Oral defence}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item if you cannot explain a line of your code, it does not count as your work
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

%=============================================================================
\section{Why Financial Markets?}
%=============================================================================

\begin{frame}{What a Financial Market Does}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Financial market}: a place or a system where buyers and sellers exchange claims on future cash flows (shares, bonds, currencies, contracts, tokens) at prices set by supply and demand
    \item \textbf{Five functions}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \textbf{capital allocation}: savings reach firms and governments
        \item \textbf{risk sharing}: risks move to those willing to carry them
        \item \textbf{liquidity}: an asset can be turned into cash quickly
        \item \textbf{price discovery}: prices gather information spread across many traders
        \item \textbf{payments and settlement}: trades are completed safely
    \end{itemize}
    \item For a statistician, the market is a data generator: every trade leaves a price and a time
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Who Trades}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.50\textwidth}
\centering
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tikzpicture}[font=\scriptsize, bx/.style={text=black, rounded corners, thick, align=center, minimum width=2.1cm, minimum height=0.9cm}]
\node[bx, draw=Forest, fill=Forest!8] (s) at (0,0) {Savers\\{\tiny households, pension funds}};
\node[bx, draw=MainBlue, fill=MainBlue!8] (i) at (3.2,0) {Intermediaries\\{\tiny banks, funds, brokers}};
\node[bx, draw=IDAred, fill=IDAred!8] (f) at (6.4,0) {Issuers\\{\tiny firms, governments}};
\node[bx, draw=Purple, fill=Purple!8, minimum width=7.4cm] (v) at (3.2,-1.7) {Venues: exchanges, dealers, clearing houses};
\draw[-{Latex}, thick, Forest] (s) -- node[above]{money} (i);
\draw[-{Latex}, thick, Forest] (i) -- node[above]{capital} (f);
\draw[-{Latex}, thick, IDAred] (f.north) to[bend right=30] node[above]{shares, bonds} (s.north);
\draw[{Latex}-{Latex}, thick, Purple] (i) -- (v);
\end{tikzpicture}}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.47\textwidth}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Buy side}: investors who buy assets: individuals (retail), pension funds, insurers, asset managers
    \item \textbf{Passive} or \textbf{active} investing
    \begin{itemize}
        \item passive: copy an index, for example through an ETF (exchange-traded fund, a fund traded like a share)
        \item active: try to beat the index
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Sell side}: brokers execute orders; market makers quote a buy and a sell price all day
\end{itemize}
\end{column}
\end{columns}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Asset Classes}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\footnotesize
\begin{tabular}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{2.2cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{4.0cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{2.8cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{3.2cm}}
\toprule
\textbf{Class} & \textbf{Examples} & \textbf{Cash flow} & \textbf{Main risks} \\
\midrule
Equities & shares, equity ETFs & dividends & market, firm \\
Bonds & government and corporate bonds & coupons, principal & interest rate, credit \\
Currencies (FX) & EUR/USD, EUR/RON & interest differential & currency, policy \\
Commodities & gold, oil & none & supply, storage \\
Derivatives & futures, options & contingent payoffs & leverage, counterparty \\
Crypto assets & Bitcoin, Ether & none & volatility, regulation \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\begin{itemize}
    \item FX (foreign exchange): the currency market; EUR/RON = lei paid for one euro
    \item One statistical toolbox for all of them: returns, volatility, tails and dependence
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{How a Price Is Formed: the Order Book}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.42\textwidth}
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}[x=0.5cm, y=0.36cm]
\foreach \p/\q in {1/3, 2/5, 3/4} { \fill[Forest!70] (-\q, -\p) rectangle (0, -\p+0.8); \node[left, font=\tiny] at (-\q, -\p+0.4) {\q}; }
\node[right, font=\tiny] at (0.1, -0.6) {99.99}; \node[right, font=\tiny] at (0.1, -1.6) {99.98}; \node[right, font=\tiny] at (0.1, -2.6) {99.97};
\foreach \p/\q in {1/2, 2/4, 3/6} { \fill[IDAred!70] (-\q, \p) rectangle (0, \p+0.8); \node[left, font=\tiny] at (-\q, \p+0.4) {\q}; }
\node[right, font=\tiny] at (0.1, 1.4) {100.01}; \node[right, font=\tiny] at (0.1, 2.4) {100.02}; \node[right, font=\tiny] at (0.1, 3.4) {100.03};
\draw[dashed, MainBlue] (-7, 0.4) -- (2.5, 0.4);
\node[font=\scriptsize, IDAred] at (-3.5, 5) {asks (sell orders)};
\node[font=\scriptsize, Forest] at (-3.5, -4.2) {bids (buy orders)};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.55\textwidth}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Order book}: all waiting buy orders (\textbf{bids}) and sell orders (\textbf{asks}), sorted by price; bars show quantities
    \item \textbf{Bid--ask spread}: best ask minus best bid, here $100.01 - 99.99 = 0.02$, the cost of trading at once
    \item A \textbf{market order} buys or sells at once at the best prices available
    \item \textbf{Questions for the room}: a market order to buy 5 units arrives
    \begin{itemize}
        \item at what average price is it filled?
        \item what is the spread afterwards?
    \end{itemize}
    \pause
    \item \textbf{Answer}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item 2 units at 100.01 and 3 at 100.02: average $(2 \times 100.01 + 3 \times 100.02)/5 = 100.016$
        \item the best ask becomes 100.02, the spread widens to 0.03: the order moved the price
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{column}
\end{columns}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Why Statistics?}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Tomorrow's price is uncertain}: we model it as a random variable
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $P_t$: the price on day $t$; the sequence $P_1, P_2, \ldots$ is a \textbf{time series}
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{What we measure in this course}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \textbf{return}: the relative change of the price (\sfmchlink{https://danpele.github.io/SFM/EN/Courses/chapter1_data_returns_indicators.pdf}{Chapter 1})
        \item \textbf{distribution} of returns, and how heavy its tails are (\sfmchlink{https://danpele.github.io/SFM/EN/Courses/chapter2_classical_distributions_stylised_facts.pdf}{Chapters 2}, \sfmchlink{https://danpele.github.io/SFM/EN/Courses/chapter3_alpha_stable_distributions.pdf}{3} and \sfmchlink{https://danpele.github.io/SFM/EN/Courses/chapter5_heavy_tails_evt.pdf}{5})
        \item \textbf{volatility}: the standard deviation of returns, and how it changes in time (\sfmchlink{https://danpele.github.io/SFM/EN/Courses/chapter8_volatility_estimators.pdf}{Chapters 8} and \sfmchlink{https://danpele.github.io/SFM/EN/Courses/chapter9_arch_garch_models.pdf}{9})
        \item \textbf{risk measures}: VaR (Value at Risk) and ES (Expected Shortfall) (\sfmchlink{https://danpele.github.io/SFM/EN/Courses/chapter10_var_es_backtesting.pdf}{Chapter 10})
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{The big question}: can past prices predict future returns?
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the efficient market hypothesis says: hardly (\sfmchlink{https://danpele.github.io/SFM/EN/Courses/chapter7_efficient_markets_random_walk_vr.pdf}{Chapter 7})
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Recap: Why financial markets?}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Markets allocate capital, share risk, provide liquidity and discover prices
    \item Prices come from the order book: the spread is the cost of trading at once
    \item Six asset classes, one statistical toolbox
    \item Tomorrow's price is a random variable: statistics describes its returns, volatility and risk
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Risk and Return: Interpretation}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Stock indices cluster} around 15--22\% volatility a year
    \begin{itemize}
        \item returns between 5.0\% (WIG20, Warsaw) and 16.6\% (Nasdaq 100) a year
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Crypto assets are far to the right}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item Bitcoin 66.7\%, Ether 106.4\% volatility a year
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Long US government bonds (TLT) lost money}: \ensuremath{-}1.1\% a year
    \begin{itemize}
        \item TLT: an ETF of US Treasury bonds with more than 20 years to maturity; interest rates rose sharply in 2022
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Question for the room}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item does the chart prove that higher risk brings higher return?
    \end{itemize}
    \pause
    \item \textbf{Answer}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item no: these are averages of one sample; a mean return over 11 years is estimated with a large error, as \sfmchlink{https://danpele.github.io/SFM/EN/Courses/chapter1_data_returns_indicators.pdf}{Chapter 1} shows
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Crises and Drawdowns, 2000--2026}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.94\textwidth,height=0.56\textheight,keepaspectratio]{sfm_ch0_drawdowns.pdf}
\end{center}
\vspace{-2mm}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \hypertarget{ch0-dd}{}\textbf{Drawdown}: the loss from the highest previous price, $DD_t = P_t / \max_{s \le t} P_s - 1$
    \item $\max_{s \le t} P_s$: the highest price up to day $t$; $DD_t \le 0$, and $DD_t = 0$ at a new high
\end{itemize}
\sfmquantlet{Ch_00}{SFM_ch0_drawdowns}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Drawdowns: Interpretation}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{2008 global financial crisis}: the deepest fall of both indices
    \begin{itemize}
        \item S\&P 500: \ensuremath{-}56.8\% at 9 March 2009, from the peak of 9 October 2007
        \item BET: \ensuremath{-}82.5\% at 25 February 2009, from the peak of 24 July 2007
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Later crises}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item COVID-19, 2020: S\&P 500 \ensuremath{-}33.9\%, BET \ensuremath{-}34.9\%
        \item rate rises, 2022: S\&P 500 \ensuremath{-}25.4\%, BET \ensuremath{-}22.9\%
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Question for the room}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item how long did each index need to regain its 2007 peak?
    \end{itemize}
    \pause
    \item \textbf{Answer}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item S\&P 500: until 28 March 2013; BET: until 16 March 2021, more than 13 years
        \item a deep loss needs a large gain to recover: after $-80\%$, the price must grow five times
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{The Fear Index: VIX, 2000--2026}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.94\textwidth,height=0.62\textheight,keepaspectratio]{sfm_ch0_vix.pdf}
\end{center}
\vspace{-2mm}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{VIX}: the volatility of the S\&P 500 over the next 30 days expected by option traders, in \% a year (\refCboe; \refWhaley)
\end{itemize}
\sfmquantlet{Ch_00}{SFM_ch0_vix}

\begin{frame}{The VIX: Interpretation}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Usually calm}: mean 19.8, median 17.8 since 2000
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the mean is above the median: rare spikes pull it up
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Two spikes above 80}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item 20 November 2008: 80.9, two months after the bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers
        \item 16 March 2020: 82.7, the COVID-19 market panic
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Volatility comes in waves}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item high values are followed by high values, and they fade slowly
        \item this \emph{volatility clustering} is modelled with GARCH (Generalised AutoRegressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity) in \sfmchlink{https://danpele.github.io/SFM/EN/Courses/chapter9_arch_garch_models.pdf}{Chapter 9}
    \end{itemize}
    \item On 18 September 2026 the VIX closed at 14.8: a calm market
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{The Romanian Market: BET since 1997}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.94\textwidth,height=0.58\textheight,keepaspectratio]{sfm_ch0_bet_history.pdf}
\end{center}
\vspace{-2mm}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{BET}: the reference index of the BVB, launched on 19 September 1997 at 1\,000 points (\refBVB)
    \item 18 September 2026: 32\,758 points, about $\times$32.8 in 29 years, without dividends
\end{itemize}
\sfmquantlet{Ch_00}{SFM_ch0_bet_history}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{The Romanian Market: Interpretation}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Three phases}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item 1997--1999: a young market loses most of its value
        \item 2000--2007: strong growth before the EU (European Union) accession of 2007
        \item 2008--2009: a drawdown of \ensuremath{-}82.5\%, then a slow recovery and new highs in 2025--2026
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Crashes on the BVB can be modelled}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item log-periodic models fitted to the BET before 2008 (\refPeleBVB)
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Why BET-TR in comparisons}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item Romanian firms pay large dividends; an index without them understates the investor's gain
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Crypto Assets in 2026}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.62\textwidth}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Bitcoin}: proposed in 2008 (\refNakamoto) as electronic cash without a bank; traded since 2010
    \item \textbf{Closer to mainstream finance}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item January 2024: the SEC (Securities and Exchange Commission, the US market regulator) approves spot Bitcoin ETFs (\refSEC)
        \item are cryptos becoming an alternative asset class? (\refPeleCrypto)
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Still a different statistical world}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item volatility 66.7\% a year since 2015, against 17.7\% for the S\&P 500
        \item trades 24 hours a day, 7 days a week: annualise with 365 days
    \end{itemize}
    \item \sfmchlink{https://danpele.github.io/SFM/EN/Courses/chapter14_crypto_assets.pdf}{Chapter 14} is about crypto assets
\end{itemize}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.34\textwidth}
\centering
\includegraphics[height=0.6\textheight]{ch0_bitcoin_whitepaper.jpg}\\[1mm]
\imgcap{The Bitcoin white paper, 2008}
\imgcredit{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bitcoin-whitepaper-poster_page-0001.jpg}{Text: Satoshi Nakamoto (2008); poster: DailyCoinPost (2018); CC0; Wikimedia Commons}

\end{columns}

\begin{frame}{Recap: markets in 2026}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Since 2015: stock indices about 15--22\% volatility a year, Bitcoin about 66.7\%
    \item Drawdowns can be deep and long: BET \ensuremath{-}82.5\% in 2009, recovered only in 2021
    \item Volatility comes in waves: the VIX spiked above 80 in 2008 and 2020
    \item A ranking of markets depends on the window: every average is an estimate
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\section{A Short History of Markets}
%=============================================================================

\begin{frame}{Four Centuries in One Line}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[x=0.0295cm, y=0.6cm, font=\tiny]
\draw[-{Latex}, thick, MainBlue] (1590,0) -- (2035,0);
\foreach \y in {1600,1700,1800,1900,2000} { \draw[MainBlue] (\y,-0.08) -- (\y,0.08); \node[anchor=north west, xshift=1pt, text=black] at (\y,-0.1) {\y}; }
\foreach \y/\t/\c/\h in {1602/{VOC shares,\\Amsterdam}/Forest/0.9, 1637/{tulip mania}/IDAred/1.8, 1720/{South Sea bubble}/IDAred/0.9, 1792/{NYSE origins}/Forest/1.8, 1882/{Bucharest\\exchange}/Forest/0.9, 1900/{Bachelier}/MainBlue/2.7, 1929/{Black\\Tuesday}/IDAred/1.5, 1970/{Fama}/MainBlue/2.7, 1987/{Black\\Monday}/IDAred/1.4, 2008/{Lehman; Bitcoin}/IDAred/3.6}
{ \draw[\c, thick] (\y,0) -- (\y,\h); \fill[\c] (\y,0) circle (1.2pt); \node[above, text=black, align=center] at (\y,\h) {\y\\\t}; }
\draw[IDAred, thick] (2020,0) -- (2020,0.9); \fill[IDAred] (2020,0) circle (1.2pt); \node[anchor=south west, text=black, align=left, xshift=-3pt] at (2020,0.9) {2020\\COVID-19};
\foreach \y/\t/\c/\h in {1952/{Markowitz}/MainBlue/-0.9, 1995/{BVB reopens}/Forest/-1.6}
{ \draw[\c, thick] (\y,0) -- (\y,\h); \fill[\c] (\y,0) circle (1.2pt); \node[below, text=black, align=center] at (\y,\h) {\y\\\t}; }
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textcolor{Forest}{Green}: exchanges; \textcolor{IDAred}{red}: bubbles and crashes; \textcolor{MainBlue}{blue}: statistical models of prices
    \item Exchanges, crashes and models grew together: each crisis brought new data and new questions
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{The First Exchanges: from Bruges to New York}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.40\textwidth}
\centering
\includegraphics[height=0.52\textheight]{ch0_amsterdam_beurs_1612.jpg}\\[1mm]
\imgcap{The Amsterdam exchange of Hendrick de Keyser, 1612}
\imgcredit{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bird\%27s-eye_view_of_the_Beurs_van_Hendrick_de_Keyser_by_Claes_Jansz._Visscher_(II)_1612_Stadsarchief_Amsterdam_010001000620.jpg}{Engraving: Claes Jansz.\ Visscher (1612); public domain; Stadsarchief Amsterdam, Wikimedia Commons}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.57\textwidth}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Bruges}, 13th--15th centuries: merchants meet in front of the inn of the Van der Beurse family; the name becomes \emph{bourse}, \emph{bursă} (\refGelderblom)
    \item \textbf{Amsterdam}, 1602: the Dutch East India Company (VOC) issues shares that anyone can buy and resell
    \begin{itemize}
        \item continuous trading, forwards and short selling follow within a decade (\refGJ)
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{London}: from 1698, price lists published at Jonathan's Coffee House (\refNeal)
    \item \textbf{New York}, 17 May 1792: 24 brokers sign the Buttonwood Agreement, origin of the NYSE (New York Stock Exchange) (\refSWC)
\end{itemize}
\end{column}
\end{columns}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{The First Bubbles}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.36\textwidth}
\centering
\includegraphics[height=0.2\textheight]{ch0_tulip_satire_1640.jpg}\\[1mm]
\imgcap{Jan Brueghel the Younger, \emph{Satire on Tulip Mania}, c.\ 1640}
\imgcredit{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Jan_Brueghel_the_Younger,_Satire_on_Tulip_Mania,_c._1640.jpg}{Painting: Jan Brueghel the Younger (c.\ 1640); public domain; Wikimedia Commons}\\[1mm]
\centering
\includegraphics[height=0.2\textheight]{ch0_south_sea_1721.jpg}\\[1mm]
\imgcap{William Hogarth, \emph{The South Sea Scheme}, 1721}
\imgcredit{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:William_Hogarth,_The_South_Sea_Scheme,_1721,_NGA_30435.jpg}{Print: William Hogarth (1721); CC0; National Gallery of Art, Wikimedia Commons}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.60\textwidth}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Bubble}: a price far above any reasonable value of the asset, followed by a collapse
    \item \textbf{Tulip mania}, Holland, 1636--1637: tulip bulb contracts rise many times, then collapse in February 1637
    \begin{itemize}
        \item later research: a smaller episode than the legend, with few bankruptcies (\refGarber; \refGoldgar)
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{1720}: the Mississippi Company in Paris and the South Sea Company in London rise and fall within months
    \begin{itemize}
        \item prices rose most for firms tied to a real innovation, Atlantic trade and insurance (\refFGR)
    \end{itemize}
    \item Recurring ingredients: a new story, cheap credit, then forced selling
\end{itemize}
\end{column}
\end{columns}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Black Tuesday, 1929}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.36\textwidth}
\centering
\includegraphics[height=0.58\textheight]{ch0_nyse_crowd_1929.jpg}\\[1mm]
\imgcap{Crowd outside the NYSE, 29 October 1929}
\imgcredit{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Crowd_outside_nyse.jpg}{Photo: U.S.\ government (1929); public domain; Wikimedia Commons}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.60\textwidth}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{24--29 October 1929}: the New York market crashes; 29 October is \textbf{Black Tuesday}
    \item \textbf{The Great Depression}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the US contraction that began in August 1929 lasted until March 1933 (\refNBER)
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Consequences for statistics}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item stricter rules on disclosure: firms must publish regular, audited data
        \item long drawdowns are not new: the BET needed 13 years after 2008
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{column}
\end{columns}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{From the Trading Floor to Screens}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.40\textwidth}
\centering
\includegraphics[height=0.27\textheight]{ch0_nyse_floor_1963.jpg}\\[1mm]
\imgcap{The NYSE trading floor, 1963}
\imgcredit{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:NY_stock_exchange_traders_floor_LC-U9-10548-6.jpg}{Photo: Thomas J.\ O'Halloran (1963); public domain; Library of Congress, Wikimedia Commons}\\[1mm]
\centering
\includegraphics[height=0.17\textheight]{ch0_edison_ticker.jpg}\\[1mm]
\imgcap{A stock ticker of Thomas Edison}
\imgcredit{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Thomas_Edison_stock_ticker_NMAH-JN2014-3625.jpg}{Photo: Jaclyn Nash, Smithsonian (2014); public domain; Wikimedia Commons}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.57\textwidth}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Stock ticker}, from 1867: prices travel by telegraph, printed on paper strips
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the first time series of prices available outside the exchange
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Trading floor}: brokers shout orders in the pit
    \begin{itemize}
        \item prices recorded on paper by clerks
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Electronic trading}, from the 1970s--1990s
    \begin{itemize}
        \item every order and every trade is stored, to the microsecond
        \item algorithms send a large share of the orders on major exchanges
    \end{itemize}
    \item More data made new statistics possible, from daily returns to intraday volatility
\end{itemize}
\end{column}
\end{columns}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{The Bucharest Stock Exchange}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.30\textwidth}
\centering
\includegraphics[height=0.27\textheight]{ch0_bvb_palace_1928.jpg}\\[1mm]
\imgcap{Brokers at the Stock Exchange Palace, March 1928}
\imgcredit{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Nicolae_Ionescu_-_The_Stock_Exchange_Palace_in_March_1928.jpg}{Photo: Nicolae Ionescu (1928); public domain; Wikimedia Commons}\\[1mm]
\centering
\includegraphics[height=0.16\textheight]{ch0_bvb_palace_2023.jpg}\\[1mm]
\imgcap{The same building in 2023}
\imgcredit{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bucure\%C8\%99ti_-_Palatul_Bursei_(2023)_-_img_01.jpg}{Photo: Chainwit.\ (2023); CC BY 4.0; Wikimedia Commons}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.66\textwidth}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{1 December 1882}: the Bucharest exchange opens under a decree of King Carol I (\refBVB)
    \item \textbf{1948}: trading stops under the communist regime; almost 50 years without an exchange
    \item \textbf{20 November 1995}: the first session of the re-established BVB, with 6 listed companies
    \item \textbf{1997}: the BET index starts at 1\,000 points
    \item \textbf{2020}: FTSE Russell, a global index provider, upgrades Romania to Secondary Emerging market
    \item \textbf{July 2023}: Hidroelectrica, the largest IPO (initial public offering) in BVB history
\end{itemize}
\end{column}
\end{columns}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Statistics Enters Finance (1/2): Random Walks and Wild Prices}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}
\centering
\includegraphics[height=0.32\textheight]{ch0_bachelier.jpg}\\[1mm]
\imgcap{Louis Bachelier (1870--1946)}
\imgcredit{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:LouisBachelier.jpg}{Photo: unknown author; public domain; Wikimedia Commons}\\[1mm]
\raggedright
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{1900}: in his doctoral thesis, Bachelier models Paris bond prices as a \textbf{random walk} (\refBachelier)
    \item price changes: independent, with the Normal distribution
\end{itemize}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}
\centering
\includegraphics[height=0.32\textheight]{ch0_mandelbrot_2007.jpg}\\[1mm]
\imgcap{Benoit Mandelbrot (1924--2010)}
\imgcredit{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Benoit_Mandelbrot_mg_1804-d.jpg}{Photo: Rama (2007); CC BY-SA 2.0 fr; Wikimedia Commons}\\[1mm]
\raggedright
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{1963}: Mandelbrot shows that cotton price changes have far heavier tails than the Normal distribution (\refMandelbrot)
    \item he proposes the $\alpha$-stable distributions of \sfmchlink{https://danpele.github.io/SFM/EN/Courses/chapter3_alpha_stable_distributions.pdf}{Chapter 3}
\end{itemize}
\end{column}
\end{columns}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Statistics Enters Finance (2/2): Risk, Efficiency, Volatility}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.62\textwidth}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{1952}: Markowitz measures risk by the variance of returns and builds diversified portfolios (\refMarkowitz)
    \begin{itemize}
        \item risk becomes a number that can be estimated
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{1970}: Fama defines the \textbf{efficient market}: prices reflect all available information (\refFama)
    \begin{itemize}
        \item testable with statistics: are returns predictable? (\sfmchlink{https://danpele.github.io/SFM/EN/Courses/chapter7_efficient_markets_random_walk_vr.pdf}{Chapter 7})
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{1973}: Black and Scholes price options, with volatility as the key input (\refBS)
    \item \textbf{1982}: Engle models volatility that changes over time: ARCH (AutoRegressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity) (\refEngle)
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the start of \sfmchlink{https://danpele.github.io/SFM/EN/Courses/chapter8_volatility_estimators.pdf}{Chapters 8}--\sfmchlink{https://danpele.github.io/SFM/EN/Courses/chapter10_var_es_backtesting.pdf}{10}
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{column}

\end{frame}

    \item \textbf{19 October 1987, Black Monday}: the Dow Jones falls 22.6\% in one day; large falls in every major market (\refRoll)
    \item \textbf{15 September 2008}: Lehman Brothers goes bankrupt; the global financial crisis
    \begin{itemize}
        \item risk models that assumed Normal returns underestimated the losses
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{March 2020}: the COVID-19 crash
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the S\&P 500 log return is \ensuremath{-}12.8\% on 16 March 2020, its worst day since 2000
    \end{itemize}
    \item Lesson for this course: extreme days are part of the data, not errors to be removed
\end{itemize}
\end{column}

\begin{frame}{Recap: a short history}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Exchanges since the 1600s; bubbles and crashes almost from the start
    \item The Bucharest exchange: 1882--1948, then again from 1995; the BET since 1997
    \item Models: random walk (1900), portfolio risk (1952), heavy tails (1963), efficiency (1970), changing volatility (1982)
    \item Each crisis showed that extreme days are more frequent than the Normal distribution predicts
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}


%=============================================================================
\section{From Prices to Returns: a First Look}
%=============================================================================

\begin{frame}{Simple and Log Returns}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item $P_t$: the price at the end of day $t$ (for ETFs and shares, the price adjusted for dividends and splits); $P_{t-1}$: the price of the previous day
    \item \textbf{Simple return}: $R_t = \dfrac{P_t}{P_{t-1}} - 1$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the percentage gain of one day: what the investor earns
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Log return}: $r_t = \ln \dfrac{P_t}{P_{t-1}} = \ln(1 + R_t)$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $\ln$: the natural logarithm; $r_t$ is the continuously compounded return of the day
        \item almost equal to $R_t$ for small moves; smaller for large ones
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Worked example}: $P_0 = 100$, $P_1 = 110$, $P_2 = 99$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $R_1 = +10\%$, $r_1 = \ln 1.1 = +$9.53\%
        \item $R_2 = -10\%$, $r_2 = \ln 0.9 = $ \ensuremath{-}10.54\%
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Which Returns Add Up?}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Questions for the room}: same example, $100 \to 110 \to 99$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item what is the sum of the two simple returns?
        \item did the investor gain, lose or break even over the two days?
    \end{itemize}
    \pause
    \item \textbf{Answer}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $R_1 + R_2 = 10\% - 10\% = 0\%$, but the investor lost: $99/100 - 1 = -1\%$
        \item simple returns \textbf{compound}: $(1 + R_1)(1 + R_2) - 1 = 1.1 \times 0.9 - 1 = -1\%$
        \item log returns \textbf{add}: $r_1 + r_2 = $ \ensuremath{-}1.01\% $= \ln(99/100)$
    \end{itemize}
    \item Rule: add log returns over time; compound simple returns (details in \sfmchlink{https://danpele.github.io/SFM/EN/Courses/chapter1_data_returns_indicators.pdf}{Chapter 1})
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Mean, Volatility and Annualisation}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{itemize}
    \item From $n$ daily log returns $r_1, \ldots, r_n$
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \textbf{mean}: $\bar r = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{t=1}^n r_t$
        \item \textbf{volatility}: the standard deviation $s = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{t=1}^n (r_t - \bar r)^2}$
        \item $s$: the typical distance of a daily return from its mean; dividing by $n-1$ instead of $n$ corrects for $\bar r$ being estimated from the same data
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Annualisation} with $A$ observations per year
    \begin{itemize}
        \item mean: $A \bar r$, because log returns add up; volatility: $\sqrt{A}\, s$, because the variances of independent days add up
        \item $A \approx 252$ for exchanges, $A = 365$ for Bitcoin
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Worked example}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item a stock index with daily volatility 1\%: $\sqrt{252} \times 1\% = $ 15.9\% a year
        \item Bitcoin with daily volatility 3\%: $\sqrt{365} \times 3\% = $ 57.3\% (with 252 by mistake: 47.6\%)
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{S\&P 500 Daily Returns, 2000--2026}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.94\textwidth,height=0.62\textheight,keepaspectratio]{sfm_ch0_returns.pdf}
\end{center}
\vspace{-2mm}
\begin{itemize}
    \item 6\,714 daily log returns, from 4 January 2000 to 18 September 2026
\end{itemize}
\sfmquantlet{Ch_00}{SFM_ch0_returns}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Daily Returns: Interpretation}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Small on average, large in crises}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item mean 0.025\% a day, standard deviation 1.21\% a day (19.2\% a year)
        \item worst day: \ensuremath{-}12.8\% on 16 March 2020; best day: +11.0\% on 13 October 2008
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Volatility clustering}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item large moves come in groups: 2002, 2008--2009, 2020, 2022, April 2025
        \item the best and the worst days are close in time
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{The mean is hard to see}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the daily mean is about 49 times smaller than the daily standard deviation
        \item estimating expected returns needs long samples; estimating volatility is much easier
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Returns versus the Normal Distribution}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.94\textwidth,height=0.6\textheight,keepaspectratio]{sfm_ch0_histogram.pdf}
\end{center}
\vspace{-2mm}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Histogram of the S\&P 500 daily log returns since 2000; red: the Normal density with the same mean and variance; vertical log scale
\end{itemize}
\sfmquantlet{Ch_00}{SFM_ch0_returns}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Heavy Tails: Interpretation}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{More extreme days than the Normal distribution allows}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item days with a move larger than 4 standard deviations: 46 observed
        \item expected under the Normal distribution with the same mean and variance: 0.43
        \item the worst day, 16 March 2020, lies \ensuremath{-}10.5 standard deviations from the mean
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Kurtosis} $K = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^n (r_t - \bar r)^4 / s^4$: the mean fourth power of the standardised returns
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $(r_t - \bar r)/s$: distance from the mean in standard deviations; the fourth power lets the extreme days dominate $K$
        \item Normal distribution: $K = 3$; S\&P 500 since 2000: 13.7; $K > 3$ means heavier tails than the Normal
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Also more quiet days}: the histogram is taller in the centre
    \begin{itemize}
        \item risk measured with the Normal distribution is too low in the tails (\sfmchlink{https://danpele.github.io/SFM/EN/Courses/chapter2_classical_distributions_stylised_facts.pdf}{Chapters 2}, \sfmchlink{https://danpele.github.io/SFM/EN/Courses/chapter5_heavy_tails_evt.pdf}{5} and \sfmchlink{https://danpele.github.io/SFM/EN/Courses/chapter10_var_es_backtesting.pdf}{10})
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Drawdown, Step by Step}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.38\textwidth}
\begin{center}
\footnotesize
\begin{tabular}{rrrr}
\toprule
$t$ & $P_t$ & peak $M_t$ & $DD_t$ \\
\midrule
0 & 100 & 100 & $0\%$ \\
1 & 120 & 120 & $0\%$ \\
2 & 90 & 120 & $-25\%$ \\
3 & 110 & 120 & $-8.3\%$ \\
4 & 130 & 130 & $0\%$ \\
5 & 104 & 130 & $-20\%$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.58\textwidth}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Running peak}: $M_t = \max_{s \le t} P_s$, the highest price over the days $s = 0, \ldots, t$
    \item \textbf{Drawdown} (\hyperlink{ch0-dd}{\textcolor{MainBlue}{defined with the crises chart}}): $DD_t = P_t / M_t - 1$
    \item \textbf{Maximum drawdown} (MDD): the most negative $DD_t$; here $-25\%$, from 120 to 90
    \item \textbf{Why investors watch it}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item it is the loss of someone who bought at the worst moment
        \item it ignores how long the recovery takes: report the duration too
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{column}
\end{columns}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Recap: from prices to returns}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item $R_t = P_t/P_{t-1} - 1$ compounds; $r_t = \ln(P_t/P_{t-1})$ adds up over time
    \item Annualise the mean with $A$ and the volatility with $\sqrt{A}$; $A = 365$ for Bitcoin
    \item Daily returns: volatility clustering and heavy tails (kurtosis 13.7 against 3)
    \item Drawdown: the loss from the previous peak; the maximum drawdown summarises the worst episode
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}


%=============================================================================
\section{AI for Scientific Discovery}
%=============================================================================

\begin{frame}{An Open Question}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Question}: has Bitcoin become less volatile since it entered mainstream finance?
    \item \textbf{Why it matters}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item a less volatile Bitcoin would be easier to hold in a pension fund or a bank portfolio
        \item the spot ETFs of January 2024 opened Bitcoin to investors who buy through ordinary brokerage accounts (\refSEC)
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Why it is open}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item only a few years of data after 2024
        \item other explanations exist: a calmer market overall, a larger and more liquid market
        \item related evidence: cryptos and traditional assets move closer over time (\refPeleCrypto)
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{How AI Could Help}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Literature}: ask for peer-reviewed papers on Bitcoin volatility, with DOIs
    \begin{itemize}
        \item then open every DOI yourself: AI assistants invent plausible references
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Hypotheses}: ask for three competing explanations of a fall in volatility
    \begin{itemize}
        \item each explanation should predict something the others do not
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Code}: ask for a first draft that computes the volatility per year
    \begin{itemize}
        \item check the annualisation, the calendar and the dates line by line
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Critique}: ask the assistant to act as a hostile referee of your result
    \begin{itemize}
        \item machine learning can generate hypotheses; testing them stays a human job (\refLM)
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Mini-Case: Volatility per Year}
\itemsize{\footnotesize}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.94\textwidth,height=0.52\textheight,keepaspectratio]{sfm_ch0_btc_vol.pdf}
\end{center}
\vspace{-2mm}
\begin{itemize}
    \item Annualised volatility of daily log returns in each calendar year; Bitcoin with 365 days, the S\&P 500 with its own frequency; 2026*: until 18 September
    \item Bitcoin: average 69.6\% a year in 2015--2023, 47.3\% in 2024--2026; in 2025, 2.25 times the S\&P 500
\end{itemize}
\sfmquantlet{Ch_00}{SFM_ch0_btc_vol}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{What to Check}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Fix the comparison before looking at the chart}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item break date: the ETF approval of January 2024, not the year that looks best
        \item trying many dates and keeping the best one produces false discoveries (\refHLZ)
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Rule out the rival explanation}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item if all markets were calmer, the S\&P 500 volatility fell too: compare the ratio Bitcoin / S\&P 500
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Check the numbers}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item 365 days a year for Bitcoin; the same definition of volatility in every year
        \item one year is a short sample: a single calm year is not a trend
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Say what the result cannot show}: a fall after 2024 does not prove that the ETFs caused it
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Your Turn: a Project Seed}
\itemsize{\small}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Question}: is Bitcoin's volatility, relative to the S\&P 500, lower after January 2024 than before?
    \item \textbf{Steps}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item replicate the chart of the mini-case from the course data
        \item write down the hypothesis, the break date and the test before computing
        \item compare the variances of daily returns before and after with a test for equal variances (Levene test)
        \item repeat with Ether as a second crypto asset
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Report}
    \begin{itemize}
        \item the two volatilities, the ratio, the test result and one limitation
        \item every AI prompt that shaped a decision, in \texttt{AI\_USE.md}
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
\end{frame}
